Verifying residential projects in AI answers: developer, building, schedule and purchase terms

Alexey YakovlevUpdated 9 November 2026

Homebuyers ask about a district, budget, layout and move-in date. An AI answer can confuse the property brand, the legal developer, the individual building and a specific apartment. Each can have different documents and delivery dates.

Discuss your projectSee the service

A useful recommendation should match the buyer question to a specific project and building, with evidence for location, timeline, declaration and offer recency.

Separate the development brand, legal entity, building and unit

A marketing brand can cover multiple construction stages. Project obligations should be checked against the relevant legal entity and documentation, rather than being inferred from a shared logo. Store building identifiers, address and source dates along with the AI response.

Saying that an entire development will be ready this year is misleading when individual stages have different schedules. The buyer needs the date associated with the selected building and contractual delivery conditions.

  • Keep developer brand and legal project entity as different fields.
  • Record project, construction stage, building and offer identifiers.
  • Distinguish planned completion from applicable handover terms.
  • Attach a source date to availability and price statements.

Five unbranded purchase-intent examples

Build a baseline from real constraints: district, budget, transport, layout, delivery date and household needs. Keep prompts mentioning the project name in a separate branded group.

These are examples for designing a test set, not answers from a completed AI measurement.

  • Which new developments in this district fit a family and this budget?
  • Which buildings are scheduled for handover by a specified month?
  • What developments near a particular transit corridor offer the requested layout?
  • How do two buildings compare on dates, specification and available units?
  • Where can I verify the declaration and legal developer of this project?

Housing construction information and declarations

For projects subject to the applicable Russian shared-construction legislation, the official housing information system publishes construction materials. Article 19 of Federal Law 214-FZ covers project declarations. A published declaration does not independently certify marketing promises about finishing quality or travel times.

When descriptions disagree, inspect the current declaration, change history and the actual transaction documents. Verify each claim against its own source rather than applying a blanket verified status to a development.

  • Find the exact legal entity and building.
  • Review the current declaration and relevant amendments.
  • Match dates and characteristics to the specific stage.
  • Distinguish projected plans from completed outcomes.

A fact passport suitable for buyers and AI retrieval

A project page should expose stable facts, such as location, project identity, construction status and documentation, separately from fast-changing offers. Unit prices, stock and financing terms require a dated source.

Structured data must correspond to information actually visible to visitors. Do not add fabricated offers, ratings or delivery dates merely to populate Schema.org.

  • Project identity and address.
  • Building, stage, legal developer and documents.
  • Offer fields with update date and evidence.
  • The difference between official project facts and third-party neighbourhood opinions.

Four different outcomes from an AI response

A brand mention is not the same as a relevant building recommendation. Record the full output, cited sources and a manual assessment for each prompt and AI interface.

For BMR changes, keep the same prompt set, response denominator and classification rules. A new building or a changed test panel creates a different sample, not evidence of an automatic improvement.

  • Developer brand mentioned only.
  • Correct project or building recommended.
  • Project named but factual entity or deadline confused.
  • Answer absent or claim not verifiable at the tested date.

GAEO already has a bilingual real-estate service page and standard pricing. This guide adds a verification protocol for a specific project; it is neither a new service tariff nor evidence of a newly completed client project.

Any future narrower commercial page should be justified by genuinely distinct buyer demand and additional verifiable facts.

Frequently asked questions

Does naming the developer mean an AI service recommends the building?+
No. The answer must refer to the relevant project or building and match the location, budget and date requirements.
Can a marketing completion date be treated as verified?+
Only after checking its current supporting source and the documents applicable to the specific building and transaction.
How should multi-stage developments be evaluated?+
Treat each stage and building as a separate entity for deadlines, specifications and offers.
Does GAEO need a new developer pricing plan?+
No. The existing real-estate service and common pricing remain the commercial source.
Is this guide proof of increased AI recommendations?+
No. It provides an evidence method, not a newly measured client outcome.
